part-1-drawing-foundations/level-0.-simp.title: Level 0. Simple Fundamentals
part-1-drawing-foundations/level-0.-simp.content:
Part 1 - Drawing foundations
This is the most important stage. If you feel very lost, this teaches you how to use your eyes and hands.
My personal picks for the fundamental of construction, would be copying what you see on Peter Hans Dynamic Bible as many times as you want. Make it into a daily exercise if you feel like this is one of your main weaknesses. Grind it daily for months beside other tasks.
The Dynamic Bible - Peter Han

and as an alternative (I haven’t tried it), drawabox.

All lessonsNextLevel 1. Perspective

part-1-drawing-foundations/level-1.-pers.title: Level 1. Perspective
part-1-drawing-foundations/level-1.-pers.content:
Part 1 - Drawing foundations
Still talking about drawing in a very formal way, this can even sound boring and very mind-consuming for many, but it is a mandatory rule to understand three-dimensionality in our drawings.
Perspective can largely be developed through observation and practice.
You can go with
Framed Perspective Vol. 1 - Marcos Mateu-Mestre

or the slightly angrier cousin, way more challenging and technical in my opinion, but I really like it:
How To Draw - Scott Robertson

We will see two outlooks on human body, one more gestural with:

part-1-drawing-foundations/level-3.-ligh.title: Level 3. Light, Shadows and folds
part-1-drawing-foundations/level-3.-ligh.content:
Part 1 - Drawing foundations
Weak point of most artists, Achilles’ heel of many animators, this will probably be the longest session.
First, we learn the laws of nature and how light works with
Color and Light

Practice the real application in 3d-perspective with
Framed Perspective Vol. 2:

Something insanely demanded and very frequently overlooked by artists is how to draw clothing folds, and how they interact with the body, this one is a very quick read, we look at
Clothing folds and creases by Michel Lauricella

part-1-drawing-foundations/level-4.-not-.title: Level 4. Not the final boss
part-1-drawing-foundations/level-4.-not-.content:
Part 1 - Drawing foundations
This will carry the process of shadow blocking, specially for animation-enthusiasts

It’s a useful bridge into animation because it teaches composition, framing, clarity, and visual storytelling.
It teaches you also how to be analytical with the references you gather and the way you can look at animes and movies when watching.
And in the end of it, specific resources for those who want more control over the variables:
That one will give you the perfect understanding of painting surfaces:
How to Render:

Anatomy focused resource, you can get away with many many others:

part-2-animation-grind/getting-started-w.content:
Part 2 - Animation practice
The animation grind will be more practical, and we will work on a series of exercises after we deal with the first step.
Make sure to ask for resources and tips on the Discord server if you need anything.
My main idea is: by mastering every level on this method, your animation skills will be honed to at least satisfying level so you can freely practice and grind for life, building your portfolio for greatness.

PreviousLevel 4. Not the final bossAll lessonsNextLevel 0. Fundamentals

part-2-animation-grind/level-0.-fundamen.title: Level 0. Fundamentals
part-2-animation-grind/level-0.-fundamen.content:
Part 2 - Animation practice
www.youtube.com/watch—YKCCUMw&list=PLqKRc0Oi7q20wxXVUNiS15S2MvtSqOtLV
Really really simple playlist to get your started on how those “moving-drawings” work and what are the technicalities behind it, and some of the thought process behind creating the first little movements.
Very very good way to start, you can do one or a feel animations to try every step of the playlist, it’s gonna be very good and valuable practice.
After that, of course its The Animatorâ€™s Survival Kit, can’t run from it, it’s pretty good. Covers timing, spacing, working methods, walks, weight, dialogue, acting, there’s even videos to go along with it, and it’s really important in a beginner’s life.
Full Survival Kit video lessons: youtu.be/fuNW9vLUxu4
It will consume some hours of your life, but for me, its a must-do step. animate along with it too.
If you think this is not for you, you don’t know how much you don’t know.

part-2-animation-grind/level-1.-first-gr.title: Level 1. First Grind
part-2-animation-grind/level-1.-first-gr.content:
Part 2 - Animation practice
Let’s all grind through exercises. Pick a level for you and let’s go up forever. We criticize each other and help each other go up.
First one will be:
Ball
Animate whatever you want with a ball. If you feel like a very beginner, do your bouncing ball, try different weights.
If you feel like doing it even though you are more advanced, explore different things, use your creativity, you can do whatever you want.
Challenge yourself, surprise yourself.

PreviousLevel 0. FundamentalsAll lessonsNextLevel 2. Flour Sack

part-2-animation-grind/level-2.-flour-sa.title: Level 2. Flour Sack
part-2-animation-grind/level-2.-flour-sa.content:
Part 2 - Animation practice
The classic flour sack.
Depending on the way you want to challenge yourself, try to communicate weight with flour sack animations. Creativity is key.
There’s too many of this on Youtube, feel free to look through it if you need.

PreviousLevel 1. First GrindAll lessonsNextLevel 3. Head turn

part-2-animation-grind/level-3.-head-tur.title: Level 3. Head turn
part-2-animation-grind/level-3.-head-tur.content:
Part 2 - Animation practice
This is our first view in character acting, we should start with something simple, but aim to keep it consistent and focus on perfecting your arcs.
Challenge yourself with faster twists or change of expression if you feeling adventurous.
Also, add shadows and highlights if you are feeling fancy!
I like Dong Chang. youtu.be/7jmrUpEFpRc

PreviousLevel 2. Flour SackAll lessonsNextLevel 5. Walk Cycle

part-2-animation-grind/level-5.-walk-cyc.title: Level 5. Walk Cycle
part-2-animation-grind/level-5.-walk-cyc.content:
Part 2 - Animation practice
I feel like this is where we start to go into advanced territory. A walk cycle is the way you benchmark your ability to keep it simple but make it beautiful.
Animate a walk cycle, you can try with different characters if you want a challenge, try to give them personality. Each person walks differently, and this is a very hard and specific thing to observe and its insanely beautiful when you train your ability to translate personality in your character’s actions.
You can and probably SHOULD try a run cycle too, since we are getting into character acting territory, there’s no such thing as “too much training”.
Toshiyuki Inoue cool resource on it: pa-works.jp/howto/aruki.html

part-2-animation-grind/level-6.-lifting-.title: Level 6. Lifting heavy objects
part-2-animation-grind/level-6.-lifting-.content:
Part 2 - Animation practice
Try to explore the action behind lifting, throwing, or picking up something heavy, the speed it moves, how it moves, how a human interacts with the exertion of effort/physical strength.

PreviousLevel 5. Walk CycleAll lessonsNextLevel 7. Attack combo

part-2-animation-grind/level-7.-attack-c.title: Level 7. Attack combo
part-2-animation-grind/level-7.-attack-c.content:
Part 2 - Animation practice
Animate a short attack combo for your character, making sure you analyze the intention, body-mechanics, ways to output energy and force through attacks, weight-transfer mechanics and so on. Take it into your own hands, the internet has infinite resources. Your animation will turn out good as long as you can reach your desired intention with your drawings. Analyze your own decisions with every part of the body so your attacks are able to demonstrate the most power and are highly based on human body realistic mechanics of movement.

PreviousLevel 6. Lifting heavy objectsAll lessonsNextLevel 7.5 Effects animation

part-2-animation-grind/level-7.5-effects.title: Level 7.5 Effects animation

part-2-animation-grind/level-8.-longer-s.title: Level 8. Longer shots
part-2-animation-grind/level-8.-longer-s.content:
Part 2 - Animation practice
For level 8, now we are really going to run into the depths of animation, we are reaching levels of “doing whatever we want”, so in order to really test the capacities of this “Learning method”, we will work on longer acting and fighting scenes, 5+ seconds, use your creativity, challenge yourself, grab references, analyze masters.
Additional challenge: Fill a timesheet with it.

index.title: Studio Grind
index.content:
Studio Grind
    
      Start with drawing
      Jump to animation
    
  

Before you begin
I wanted to keep it short, this guide is a resource for those who seek directions and had a tough time deciding and building a routine, and want to practice and get better at drawing, with or without the intention of becoming a good animator.
I could spend thousands of hours researching and writing a full book, but that’s not my intention. This is not a mandatory curriculum at all.
I believe what makes a good art LEARNER is the ability to analyze your weaknesses and work on them through your whole life, being able to judge your own technical growth while practicing, always meta-thinking about WHAT WORKS and WHY is your biggest strength. You have to aim to be not only a good artist, but a good LEARNER.
I truly believe that if you “Max level” dynamic drawing, perspective, anatomy, gesture, rendering, light and shadow knowledge, you can probably become a really good artist.
You pick whatever you want. It’s a small map so we can have fun together.
You are 100% free to dislike it and hate the ideas, I am not that smart but my advice is probably valuable to some.
Intentional practice is MANDATORY, only reading will not get you far.
You should gather good references for every step. Looking at art and building your own taste and judgement for aesthetic and technicality is a huge strength.
